title: The discovery code screens on the t statistic where it means the p-value, which moves both rows of the table
location: published appendix pp. 38 to 40, and p. 851
corrected: train_pval = tidy(lm_robust(Y ~ Z * X, subset = train == 1))[4, [["p.value"]]], ... all_pval = tidy(lm_robust(Y ~ Z * X))[4, [["p.value"]]], ... Full sample Z:X [[0.24]] [[0.37]] [[0.23]] [[1.00]] [[0.00]] ... Test sample Z:X -0.00 0.41 [[0.14]] [[0.04]] [[0.77]]
note:
The columns are Bias, RMSE, Frequency, False Pos, and False Neg. The code on p. 38 computes the two screening variables as `tidy(...)[4, 4]`. Column 4 of the `tidy()` output is `statistic`, not the p-value that the variable names `train_pval` and `all_pval`, the tests `< 0.05` on p. 39, and the prose on p. 40 describe. The archived versions of estimatr from 0.10.0 (July 2018) through 0.20.0 (September 2019) have `statistic` in that column, and the deposit dates from February 2019. The deposit's saved diagnosis, `rds_files/3_10_discovery_5000_sims.rds`, shows what the published run did. The 1,438 Full sample estimates it keeps are all at or below 0.015, with a median p-value of 0.55 and only 4.8 percent below .05, so the published run kept estimates by t, not by p. The Test sample row uses the same screen, so both rows are affected. The corrected code reads `[4, "p.value"]` in both lines.

The corrected rows are the maintained replication's: the same simulated draws, screened on the p-value, with 50,000 draws because the conditional bias moves in the second decimal at the published 5,000. Screening the same draws on the statistic, as printed, gives Full sample -0.25 0.32 0.28 0.05 1.00 and Test sample 0.00 0.41 0.32 0.05 0.76, within simulation error of the printed rows, which is why the printed rows are attributed to the screen. Both maintained scripts are in the repository: `maintained/table_a18_discovery.R` reproduces the printed table from the printed code, and `maintained/table_a18_discovery_intended.R` computes both screens on the same draws and writes the corrected values. Both use complete random assignment, as the appendix describes and as the deposit's `declare_assignment(prob = 0.5)` produced. The printed code is on appendix pp. 38 and 39 and the table on pp. 39 and 40.

The article's conclusions about discovery stand. Page 851's two statements, lower bias from principled discovery and mean squared error that is not necessarily lower, hold under the corrected rows: the Test sample's bias is -0.00 against 0.24 for the Full sample, and its RMSE is 0.41 against 0.37. Page 40's prose is right as written. Under the comparison method the false positive rate is 1.00 and the false negative rate is 0.00, where the printed row says 0.05 and 1.00 and so contradicts the prose. The principled method's false positive rate is 0.04, and it often fails to reject, with a false negative rate of 0.77. Its estimates are noisier: the spread of the errors around the bias, the square root of the squared RMSE less the squared bias, is 0.41 against 0.28. It is less likely to produce a result at all, with a frequency of 0.14 against 0.23, where the printed table has the Test sample more frequent, 0.32 against 0.29. The Full sample's bias also changes sign, from negative to positive, which is the exaggeration from conditioning on significance that p. 40 describes.

title: The claim that regression performs as well as or better than the Boolean algorithms has no printed support
location: published p. 848, and appendix pp. 21 and 22
published: Using regression to perform QCA [[is equivalent to]] QMC and CCubes when there is no error, and [[even slightly outperforms]] these algorithms (on the diagnosands we consider) in the presence of measurement error. ... In such cases, the saturated regression approach [[slightly outperforms]] the Boolean minimization algorithms.
corrected: NA
note: The table on appendix p. 21 prints Correct 0.00 and Failure 1.00 for Least Squares in all four of its rows, which are error rates 0 and 0.2 at N of 3 and 50. The other two strategies print 0.10 and 0.32 for QMC and 0.10 and 0.05 for CCubes at N = 3 with no error, and 1.00 and 0.00 for both at N = 50 with no error. Page 22 has the second sentence and no table rows. A strategy that fails in every simulation cannot be read from the table as equivalent to the algorithms or as outperforming them, in either clause of the sentence on p. 848. The cause is in the code: the least squares strategy passes its predicted configurations to `QCA::simplify` inside a `try()`, `simplify` is not exported by the QCA package (checked under QCA 3.25), and every call fails, so every simulation returns "NO SOLUTION". The maintained replication reproduces the printed column for that reason, in four rows of `maintained/output/table_a11_qca_with_least_squares.csv`, all with a correct rate of 0 and a failure rate of 1. The note does not say what the least squares strategy would show if the call worked. The two claims have no support in what the article and appendix print.

note: The table on appendix p. 31 prints a bias of 0.00, with a standard error of 0.01, for every row, both the equal-probability design (`design_1`) and the unequal-probability design (`design_2`). title: The Bayesian posterior parameters are one too small, which moves the flat-prior row of the table
published: alpha <- n_successes + [[alpha_0 - 1]] ... beta <- n_trials - n_successes + [[beta_0 - 1]] ... 10 flat priors [[0.46]] [[0.14]] [[0.00]] [[-0.04]] [[-0.15]]

note: The columns are Mean Est, Mean Sd, Bias, Mean Shift, and SD Shift. A beta prior with parameters alpha_0 and beta_0 updates to a beta posterior with parameters alpha_0 plus the successes and beta_0 plus the failures, so the printed code's `- 1` makes the posterior one count too small on each side and, for the flat prior, turns the posterior mean into the sample proportion. The corrected row is computed from the sampling distribution of the number of successes in 10 draws, with the design's mean success probability. The same computation with the `- 1` reproduces the printed flat row and the printed informative row to the printed digits, which confirms that it describes the table. The informative row, 0.49 0.09 0.03 -0.01 -0.02, does not change at two decimals. The table's n = 100 rows repeat its n = 10 rows in all five columns, which is a separate defect: the declaration writes the sample size as a literal inside `declare_sampling()`, where `redesign()` cannot reach it. Entry 56 corrects those rows.
